title: Rural crime: how organised criminals exploit the countryside
label: 13 October 2026 · Rural crime and organised crime
summary: Witnesses described rural crime as diverse, often organised, and badly measured. Farmers and rural communities face theft, wildlife crime, drug-related intimidation and waste crime. Problems include poor statistics, inconsistent policing, weak intelligence sharing and under-resourcing of specialist units. Panellists urged better training, sustained funding, stronger industry partnerships, targeted technology and careful design of any police reforms so rural needs aren’t lost.

glossary.definition: A large insurer whose claims data is commonly used to estimate rural crime losses.
A small national police unit focused on rural crime coordination and best practice.
Regional Organised Crime Unit—specialist regional teams that support forces on complex organised crime.
Drug-dealing networks that move drugs and exploit people across areas; their tactics have changed recently.
A policing risk score (Management of Risk in Law Enforcement) used to prioritise ROCU work.
Automatic Number Plate Recognition cameras, used to trace vehicles.
Law intended to improve security and marking of plant and quad bikes to reduce theft.

chapters.title: How big is rural crime, and what does it include?
chapters.takeaway: Rural crime is broad, often organised, and badly measured – insurance figures are only the visible tip.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re focusing on rural crime today—how organised criminality affects farms and villages.

turns.speaker: Robyn Munt
turns.text: Farmers see theft, waste crime, hare coursing and intimidation; all disrupt farms, homes and food production.

turns.speaker: Dr Kate Tudor
turns.text: We don’t have reliable national statistics. Rural offences aren’t separated out in police data, so debates rely on NFU Mutual claims.

turns.speaker: Dr Smith
turns.text: NFU Mutual figures show one part—insured theft—but rural serious and organised crime also includes modern slavery, food fraud, agrochemical counterfeiting and cybercrime.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: Constituents say they stop reporting because cases aren’t followed up. That reduces recorded crime and hides the scale of the problem.

turns.speaker: Dr Kate Tudor
turns.text: Many rural offenders meet definitions of organised crime groups, but because they aren’t mapped as OCGs, the national picture misses them.

turns.speaker: Robyn Munt
turns.text: Reporting depends on trust with local police; where that relationship is poor, crimes go unreported and impacts—like childcare or crop timing—are greater.

turns.speaker: Dr Smith
turns.text: My rough estimates put potential insurance-relevant losses far higher than single-company figures; we’re looking at much bigger hidden costs.

chapters.title: Policing on the ground: neighbourhood teams, tech and training
chapters.takeaway: Good local policing and technology help, but capability varies wildly between forces and needs stable funding and training.

turns.speaker: Dr Prinsley
turns.text: Are named neighbourhood officers and local stations useful in rural areas, like fire stations?

turns.speaker: Dr Kate Tudor
turns.text: Named officers help if they’re competent in rural crime. Symbolic stations matter less than investigative capacity and specialist skills.

turns.speaker: Donna Jones
turns.text: In Hampshire I reintroduced named local bobbies and reopened front counters; visible presence and local bobbies reduced crime in some towns by about 19%.

turns.speaker: David Allen
turns.text: We invested 44% more in neighbourhood policing staff in Cumbria; working with local groups and WhatsApp alerts reduced quad-bike thefts by nearly half.

turns.speaker: Robyn Munt
turns.text: Technology—drones, deployable CCTV and ANPR—works well when funded and maintained, but many forces rely on short-lived grants.

turns.speaker: Dr Smith
turns.text: Neighbourhood policing builds trust and intelligence. In my surveys, rural confidence in police can be dramatically lower than urban figures.

turns.speaker: Andrew Huddleston
turns.text: Training is key: not every officer must be an expert, but they must know where to go for specialist rural knowledge. Our National Rural Crime Unit helps train officers nationally.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: Is there best practice to spread nationally?

turns.speaker: Dr Kate Tudor
turns.text: Yes: dedicated rural coordinators in each force, better intelligence collation and institutionalised rural training would help—but they need funding.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: How well do ROCUs support rural cases?

turns.speaker: Dr Kate Tudor
turns.text: ROCU support happens, but ROCUs focus on highest threat/harm. Many rural organised groups fall between local capacity and ROCU thresholds, so they slip through.

turns.speaker: Dr Smith
turns.text: That gap means regional work only reaches the most extreme rural cases, leaving persistent organised groups unaddressed.

chapters.title: County lines, wildlife crime and industry partnerships
chapters.takeaway: County lines and organised groups now use rural spaces for a wide range of crimes; industry partnerships are essential to respond.

turns.speaker: Bell Ribeiro-Addy
turns.text: How do county lines operate in rural areas now?

turns.speaker: Dr Kate Tudor
turns.text: County lines have shortened their routes and adapted: nominals from those networks commit wildlife crimes—poaching, hare coursing—that bring violence and intimidation to rural communities.

turns.speaker: Robyn Munt
turns.text: Once groups find a soft spot they return. Members report repeated assaults and day-time trespass affecting crops, livestock and access.

turns.speaker: Dr Smith
turns.text: Rural areas can also host drug production—abandoned barns become low-visibility sites for labs—and reports and evaluations have under-recognised rural roles.

turns.speaker: Andrew Huddleston
turns.text: Organised crime groups target rural areas because they can move high-value kit and hide it quickly. We saw national GPS thefts and plant thefts run across many forces; rural teams and industry funding were key to catching offenders.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: Partnerships—like Operation Scorpion—help cross borders. How important are industry partnerships?

turns.speaker: Andrew Huddleston
turns.text: Crucial. The NFU, Construction Equipment Association and insurers fund training, intelligence sharing and the National Rural Crime Unit’s co-ordination role.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: What about the Equipment Theft (Prevention) Act—why hasn’t it reduced thefts yet?

turns.speaker: Andrew Huddleston
turns.text: Implementation and manufacturer adoption take time. The Act’s measures—like better marking and immobilisation—need rollout and enforcement to deter organised thefts of tractors and quad bikes.

turns.speaker: Dr Smith
turns.text: We must also be careful around licensed cannabis sites; if not secured they can be infiltrated, so licensing must include strong protections.

chapters.title: Policy, funding and police reform: practical asks
chapters.takeaway: Panellists want stable funding, better intelligence sharing, targeted legislation and careful design of police reform so rural needs aren’t neglected.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How do you prioritise rural crime among competing urban threats?

turns.speaker: Donna Jones
turns.text: PCCs set local priorities. I funded a rural crime taskforce, mobile CCTV, drones and named local officers. That needed local investment to change focus.

turns.speaker: David Allen
turns.text: PCCs can convene partners. In Cumbria we use the ARIS fund—seized assets—to buy kit and support community prevention; prevention reduces later demand on policing.

turns.speaker: Andrew Huddleston
turns.text: Ask: strengthen the Equipment Theft Act roll-out, push for search powers and support national co-ordination so ROCUs, NCA and rural teams can act together.

turns.speaker: Dr Kate Tudor
turns.text: Police reform could help if it builds rural needs into the national operating model, but large mergers risk drawing resources to high-demand urban areas if not carefully designed.

turns.speaker: Donna Jones
turns.text: I’m not against reform, but very concerned by proposals to cut forces to a handful. Bigger isn’t automatically better for rural coverage or local accountability.

turns.speaker: David Allen
turns.text: Do the middle bit well: centralise IT and specialist functions, keep local accountability, and evolve rather than revolutionise boundaries.

turns.speaker: Robyn Munt
turns.text: Farmers need consistent responses: better recording of rural crime, trained staff in control rooms and visible outcomes to rebuild reporting and trust.

turns.speaker: Dr Smith
turns.text: Government should rural-proof reform and policies; currently rural crime is mentioned little in national planning documents despite clear harms.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final point: what one practical change would you suggest now?

turns.speaker: Andrew Huddleston
turns.text: Mandate rural crime coordinators in every force, backed by funded regional intelligence channels, to stop criminals exploiting information gaps.

turns.speaker: Donna Jones
turns.text: Invest in deployable tech and local named officers so communities see prevention and feel safe.

turns.speaker: David Allen
turns.text: Use seized funds and local convening power to boost prevention programmes and restore neighbourhood policing where it works.

turns.speaker: Dr Kate Tudor
turns.text: Improve how rural crime is recorded and shared nationally so policy and ROCU decisions match reality.

turns.speaker: Robyn Munt
turns.text: Make sure industry partnerships continue and government funds the core policing roles, not just short-term grants.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. We’ll take these recommendations forward in the inquiry.
